1861-1877

Caption This

Civil War and Reconstruction

9

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the politics, the decision, or the mistake. Never joke about enslaved or freed people, anyone’s race or religion, soldiers, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

Confederate cartoon of Lincoln

Not done

What you’re looking at: A cartoon from Norton Ch. 14 (1864). It shows President Lincoln writing the Emancipation Proclamation. A Southern artist drew it to attack Lincoln, so he filled the room with creepy things.

Heads up: This cartoon is Confederate propaganda. It was made to make Lincoln look bad for freeing enslaved people in the rebel states. Aim your joke at the spooky furniture, the little devil, or the cartoon’s over-the-top style. Never joke about enslaved or freed people.

  • What is on the table next to the inkwell?
  • Does the artist like Lincoln? How can you tell?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Emancipation Proclamation (1863)Battle of Antietam (1862)Thirteenth Amendment (1865)
Image 2 of 5

Confederate $100 bill

Not done

What you’re looking at: A paper bill from Norton Ch. 14 that says “Confederate States of America,” “Richmond, Feb. 17th, 1864,” and “One Hundred Dollars.” The Confederate government printed money like this to pay for the war.

  • Find the date and the words “Will pay to the bearer on demand.”
  • Who do you think trusted a note like this less as the war went on?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: inflationNational Banking Act (1863)Homestead Act (1862)
Image 3 of 5

Lee surrenders to Grant

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colored print from Norton Ch. 14 of General Robert E. Lee (on the right, in gray) and General Ulysses S. Grant (on the left, in blue) at a small round table. Lee is signing the surrender papers. Aim your joke at the awkward moment, not at the soldiers who fought or died.

  • Which general is signing? What is on the table next to him?
  • Do these two look like they just finished a fight? Why or why not?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Appomattox Court HouseBattle of Vicksburg (1863)Battle of Gettysburg (1863)
Image 4 of 5

Johnson impeachment ticket

Not done

What you’re looking at: A ticket from Norton Ch. 15. It says “U.S. Senate, Impeachment of the President. Admit the Bearer, March 13, 1868.” This was the first impeachment trial of a president in U.S. history. People needed a ticket to watch.

  • Read the big words in the middle. What was the Senate doing?
  • Why would people want a ticket to this?

Image 5 of 5

Cornering the gold market

Not done

What you’re looking at: A political cartoon from Norton Ch. 15 about a money scheme in 1869. A man pokes caged bulls and bears in the “N.Y. Gold Room.” In the back, a man runs out of the U.S. Treasury with a sack of gold. Norton says the poker is Jay Gould and the runner is President Ulysses S. Grant.

  • Read the signs: “N.Y. Gold Room” and “U.S. Treasury.” What is the money story?
  • Who looks scared in this picture?
